ourClaims.timeToEffect: 30–60 minutes before a demanding cognitive task
ourClaims.studySummary: Site cites 'Military research (Neri et al., 1995; Deijen et al., 1999)' and 'A 2015 meta-analysis' confirming benefits in multitasking/high-demand scenarios, benefits most pronounced under stress not rested baseline.

humanEffects.notes: Site claims military studies in sleep-deprived/cold-stressed subjects show consistent, significant cognitive maintenance.
Site claims benefits in multitasking scenarios are well replicated; effects in low-demand tasks minimal.
Site claims reduces negative mood and fatigue ratings in sleep-deprived subjects.
Site claims dopamine precursor theory suggests potential; direct motivation trials limited.

sideEffects: Possible hyperthyroid effects at very high doses

studies.title: Effect of tyrosine supplementation on clinical and healthy populations under stress or cognitive demands — A review
studies.design: narrative review (Jongkees et al.) — this is the landmark 'Jongkees 2015' review, not a formal meta-analysis
studies.population: clinical and healthy adults, mixed studies
studies.outcome: cognitive performance under stress/cognitive demand, clinical disorders, physical exercise
studies.result: Reports on TYR effectiveness 'vary considerably'. Potential for treating clinical disorders and enhancing physical exercise judged minimal. Concludes tyrosine 'does seem to effectively enhance cognitive performance, particularly in short-term stressful and/or cognitively demanding situations' but only when neurotransmitter function is intact and dopamine/norepinephrine are temporarily depleted — i.e. it is conditional, not a general enhancer.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Tyrosine improves cognitive performance and reduces blood pressure in cadets after one week of a combat training course
studies.design: RCT (Deijen et al., matches site's cited 'Deijen et al., 1999')
studies.population: military cadets in combat training, n=21 total (10 tyrosine, 11 control)
studies.dose: 2g tyrosine/day x5 days in a protein-rich drink
studies.duration: 5 days during a combat training course
studies.outcome: memory task, tracking task, mood, systolic blood pressure, plasma MHPG
studies.result: Tyrosine group performed better than carbohydrate-control group on memory and tracking tasks; tyrosine decreased systolic blood pressure. No effects on mood were found.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: The effects of tyrosine on cognitive performance during extended wakefulness
studies.design: double-blind RCT (Neri et al., matches site's cited 'Neri et al., 1995')
studies.population: healthy adults undergoing one night of sleep loss
studies.duration: single session, ~13h of continuous testing during one night of sleep loss
studies.outcome: psychomotor task performance, vigilance-task lapse probability, mood
studies.result: Tyrosine significantly ameliorated the usual performance decline on a psychomotor task and reduced lapse probability on a high-event-rate vigilance task; improvements lasted approximately 3 hours. Authors describe tyrosine as 'relatively benign' at this dose.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Effect of tyrosine on cognitive function and blood pressure under stress
studies.duration: acute, single session with 90dB noise stressor
studies.outcome: cognitive task performance, mood, heart rate, blood pressure
studies.result: Tyrosine improved performance on two stress-sensitive cognitive tasks measured 1h post-dose; decreased diastolic blood pressure at 15min (not at 1h). No effects on mood, systolic blood pressure or heart rate were found.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Tyrosine Ingestion and Its Effects on Cognitive and Physical Performance in the Heat
studies.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
studies.design: RCT, double-blind counterbalanced crossover, military-based load-carriage protocol
studies.dose: 150mg/kg body mass tyrosine (identified as equally effective as a double dose in study 1, n=21)
studies.outcome: cognitive function and physical (2.4km time trial) performance under 40°C heat stress
studies.result: NULL RESULT: despite marked elevation in serum tyrosine, exercise heat stress impaired some aspects of cognitive function and tyrosine did NOT alleviate these decrements (P>0.05); no difference in time-trial completion time between tyrosine (19.78min) and placebo (20.29min, P=0.74).
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Tyrosine negatively affects flexible-like behaviour under cognitively demanding conditions
studies.outcome: cognitive flexibility (Wisconsin Card Sorting Test) under low vs high cognitive load
studies.result: NEGATIVE RESULT: contrary to expectations, tyrosine WORSENED cognitive flexibility under the high cognitive-load condition rather than improving it.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

verdicts.claim: Cognitive Performance Under Stress — evidenceStrength strong, 'military studies in sleep-deprived and cold-stressed subjects show consistent, significant cognitive maintenance'
verdicts.reason: The claim of consistency is not supported: alongside supportive sleep-deprivation and noise-stress trials (Neri 1995, Deijen 1994/1999), a heat-stress military-protocol RCT found NO cognitive or performance benefit (Coull 2016) and another RCT found tyrosine WORSENED cognitive flexibility under high cognitive load (Robson 2019). The effect appears stressor-type-dependent, not consistent across all stress conditions.

verdicts.claim: Working Memory Under Multitasking — evidenceStrength moderate, 'benefits in multitasking scenarios are well replicated'
verdicts.reason: None of the six selected studies directly tested working memory under multitasking; a related 2024 RCT (McAllister et al., not in the top-6 list) found L-tyrosine reduced missed responses on a Stroop task during a combined VR-stress/cognitive challenge but had no effect on physiological stress markers — this is suggestive but does not establish the 'well replicated multitasking' framing the site uses.

verdicts.claim: Mood Under Sleep Deprivation — evidenceStrength moderate, 'reduces negative mood and fatigue ratings in sleep-deprived subjects'
verdicts.reason: Two of the site's own implied source studies (Deijen 1999, Deijen 1994) explicitly report 'No effects on mood were found' for tyrosine despite finding cognitive/performance benefits in the same trials — the mood claim is not supported by the studies most likely being cited.

verdicts.claim: Motivation & Drive — evidenceStrength preliminary, 'dopamine precursor theory suggests potential; direct motivation trials in healthy rested adults are limited'
verdicts.reason: No RCT directly measuring motivation/drive as an outcome was found in this search; the site's own 'preliminary/limited evidence' framing is honest and requires no correction.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Highly heterogeneous: some RCTs used flat doses (2.0g/day, matching the top of the site's 500-2000mg range), but several landmark trials used weight-based dosing of 100-150mg/kg body mass — for a 70kg adult that is roughly 7,000-10,500mg, far above the site's stated 500-2000mg range.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Clarify that the site's 500-2000mg range reflects flat-dose consumer products, while several of the classic military/stress RCTs (Neri 1995, Deijen 1994, Coull 2016) used substantially higher weight-based doses (100-150mg/kg, i.e. 7-10g for a 70kg adult) — the site's dose is not directly equivalent to the doses shown effective in the strongest stress-performance trials.

safetySignals.signal: L-Tyrosine is a direct catecholamine precursor; MAOIs block catecholamine breakdown, so the theoretical combination risk is mechanistic (not from a dedicated human interaction RCT — none was found in this search). The site's MAOI caution is a reasonable precaution but is not backed by a specific clinical trial we could verify.

gaps: No dedicated RCT on L-tyrosine + MAOI interaction was found; the caution is mechanistic/theoretical, not trial-verified — flag this distinction rather than stating it as an established interaction.

No RCT specifically comparing L-Tyrosine vs NALT (N-Acetyl-L-Tyrosine) bioavailability/efficacy for cognition was found; the site's claim that 'most evidence favours plain L-Tyrosine over NALT' could not be independently verified in this search.
The site's 'ADHD' FAQ claim ('some small studies show modest attention improvements') was not investigated in this pass and should be separately verified before publishing.
